Research problem: MVFA scores every patch against a single frozen text anchor for "normal" and one for "abnormal", each averaged over 35 generic ImageNet templates and shared by all modalities; does replacing this static anchor with an image-conditioned text anchor — a light meta-network that maps the image's global adapted feature to a small additive shift of the normal and abnormal text embeddings, trained on the source modalities — improve zero-shot anomaly classification and segmentation on unseen BMAD modalities, and how sensitive is MVFA's zero-shot performance to the choice and number of templates in the first place? The outcomes are image-level and pixel-level AUROC and PRO on each held-out modality, and the variance of these metrics across random subsets of templates.
Rationale: Limitation G5 notes that MVFA assumes one universal visual-language concept of normality across brain MRI, liver CT, retinal OCT, chest X-ray and histopathology, and provides no prompt-sensitivity analysis, while G7 notes that normal and abnormal distributions are modelled symmetrically. The related work has moved to learnable or adaptive text sides — AnomalyCLIP learns object-agnostic prompts, HieClip learns hierarchical text, AULoRA injects visual context into the text representation, and the text-adapted few-shot framework adds a text adapter — but these are evaluated mainly on industrial data or within the same medical dataset, and none isolates the effect of conditioning the text anchor on the image under strict modality-disjoint transfer in MVFA's multi-level design. Measuring template sensitivity first establishes whether the text side is a real bottleneck before adding parameters. The change is confined to the text anchor computation in the public MVFA code and is cheap to train on one GPU; the modality-disjoint protocol prevents the conditioned anchor from simply memorising the OCT appearance from the paired OCT dataset.

Target paper title: Adapting Visual-Language Models for Generalizable Anomaly Detection in Medical Images
Target paper abstract: Recent advancements in large-scale visual-language pre-trained models have led to significant progress in zero-/few-shot anomaly detection within natural image domains. However, the substantial domain divergence between natural and medical images limits the effectiveness of these methodologies in medical anomaly detection. This paper introduces a novel lightweight multi-level adaptation and comparison framework to repurpose the CLIP model for medical anomaly detection. Our approach integrates multiple residual adapters into the pre-trained visual encoder, enabling a stepwise enhancement of visual features across different levels. This multi-level adaptation is guided by multi-level, pixel-wise visual-language feature alignment loss functions, which recalibrate the model's focus from object semantics in natural imagery to anomaly identification in medical images. The adapted features exhibit improved generalization across various medical data types, even in zero-shot scenarios where the model encounters unseen medical modalities and anatomical regions during training. Our experiments on medical anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art models, with an average AUC improvement of 6.24% and 7.33% for anomaly classification, 2.03% and 2.37% for anomaly segmentation, under the zero-shot and few-shot settings, respectively. Source code is available at: https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD
Limitations to address:
- G5. Prompting is static, generic, and domain-agnostic: The text encoder is kept frozen, and the prompts consist of hand-crafted normal/abnormal state descriptions averaged over 35 ImageNet templates. This design presumes a single, universal visual-language concept of “normal” and “abnormal” that holds uniformly across imaging modalities, and it omits instance-adaptive, visually conditioned, or hybrid prompting strategies. No prompt-sensitivity analysis is provided.
- G7. Normal/anomaly disentanglement and distributional asymmetry are not made explicit: The dual- adapter design separates anomaly-classification and anomaly-segmentation features, but it does not explicitly model the compact distribution of normal samples against the comparatively diverse distribution of abnormal samples. The method relies on shared adapted features and a few-shot normal memory bank without routing mechanisms, dual normal/abnormal pathways, or many-to- one, SigLIP-style regularization.
- G13. Scalability, memory, and privacy considerations are unaddressed: The method uses a CLIP ViT-L/14 backbone and trains six separate leave-one-out models for 50 epochs each on a single RTX 3090 GPU; training and inference time, memory footprint, and parameter counts are not reported. The term “lightweight” refers only to the adapters, not to the overall system. The few-shot memory bank grows with K and with spatial resolution, yet retrieval cost and the privacy and governance implications of storing patient-derived features are not analyzed. Downscaling to a 240 × 240 resolution and processing volumetric data as 2D slices may cause small lesions and broader 3D CT/MRI context to be lost.

Problem: Is MVFA's frozen, template-averaged 'normal' text anchor a bottleneck for few-shot transfer, and can it be replaced by a support-conditioned normal anchor? First, as a precondition, we measure the sensitivity of MVFA's zero- and few-shot AUROC to the prompt templates (variance over 20 random subsets of 5, 10 and 20 of the 35 templates). If the text side matters, we replace the static normal anchor with one shifted towards the K normal support images — a light projector, trained on source modalities, maps the mean adapted feature of the support normals to an additive offset of the normal text embedding — while the abnormal side keeps several anchors (one per state description, matched many-to-one). Outcomes: few-shot image- and pixel-level AUROC and PRO on each held-out modality, and the template-sensitivity variance, under the modality-disjoint, 3-seed, 3-draw protocol.

Rationale: Reviewers noted that image-conditioned prompts already exist and asked for a different conditioning signal and an explicit hypothesis. Conditioning on the support normals, rather than on the test image, gives the anchor a modality-level notion of 'normal' without seeing anomalies, and the asymmetric many-to-one abnormal side addresses G7's distributional asymmetry. The sensitivity analysis is now a precondition that decides whether the second step is worth running.
